articles.title: South Korea Q3 GDP grows 1.0%, beating forecasts as AI chip boom lifts exports - investingLive
articles.summary: South Korea Q3 GDP grows 1.0%, beating forecasts as AI chip boom lifts exports  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- South Korea’s Q3 GDP rose 1.0% q/q vs 0.7% expected as AI chip demand lifted exports and investment, with chips driving about half of growth. Private consumption fell for the first time in nearly four years. The KOSPI rally triggered a sidecar.
The strength of the beat, and the KOSPI sidecar on a sharp rally, underline how heavily Korean assets now trade on the AI chip cycle. That cuts both ways: it supports exporters and chip names while global AI demand holds up, but leaves the market exposed to any wobble in the global AI trade. The data reinforce the Bank of Korea’s hawkish bias after its July and September hikes, which should support the won and keep pressure on short-end bond yields. Weak consumption is the main argument against further tightening, so household-sensitive sectors are likely to keep lagging.
---
South Korea is riding the AI chip boom hard enough to set off market circuit-breakers, but its households are sitting this one out.
Summary:
- South Korea’s Q3 GDP grew 1.0% q/q, beating the 0.7% forecast and up from 0.6% in Q2; y/y growth was 3.4% versus 3.0% expected
- The Bank of Korea estimates semiconductors drive about half of growth; annual growth could reach 3.7% if Q4 holds at Q3 levels
- Exports rose 2.3% and facilities investment jumped 4.1%, led by chip equipment
- Private consumption fell 0.2%, the first decline in nearly four years, hit by a stock slump and auto strikes
- Exports topped $800 billion in January to September and are on track to pass $1 trillion this year
- The KOSPI’s strong rise triggered a sidecar halt on program trading
South Korea’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as the global AI chip boom lifted exports and investment, advance Bank of Korea estimates showed on Tuesday, though weak household spending marked a notable soft spot. Gross domestic product rose 1.0% from the previous quarter, beating the 0.7% median forecast in a Reuters poll and accelerating from 0.6% in the second quarter.
Korean equities rallied strongly on the session, with the move in the KOSPI triggering a sidecar, a temporary halt on program trading that the Korea Exchange applies when index futures move sharply, to cool momentum-driven orders.
The scale of the beat was striking against the central bank’s own expectations. The Bank of Korea had forecast 0.3% growth for the quarter in August, when it projected 3.3% growth for the year. If fourth-quarter output simply holds at third-quarter levels, annual growth would now come in at around 3.7%. A central bank official estimated that semiconductors are driving about half of the economy’s growth.
Exports rose 2.3% in the quarter on demand for chips, machinery and electrical equipment, while facilities investment jumped 4.1%, led by semiconductor manufacturing equipment. South Korea’s exports topped $800 billion in the first nine months, already above last year’s full-year record, putting the country on track to become only the fourth to pass $1 trillion in a year, after the US, China and Germany.
The weak link is consumption. Private spending fell 0.2%, the first decline in nearly four years, as financial services activity dropped amid a stock market slump and car purchases fell due to strikes at major automakers. The central bank expects a gradual recovery as chip firms’ dividend payouts in the fourth quarter and employee bonuses early next year lift household incomes, though one economist cautioned that a soft labour market and restrictive interest rates limit the scope for a strong rebound. Consumer sentiment also slipped in October.
The Bank of Korea held rates last week after back-to-back hikes in July and September but kept a hawkish stance, and today’s data give it little reason to soften that. On a year-on-year basis, GDP grew 3.4%, also above the 3.0% expected.

articles.title: South Korea's Q3 Growth Hits 1.0%, Driven by Semiconductor Exports - 조선일보
articles.summary: South Korea's Q3 Growth Hits 1.0%, Driven by Semiconductor Exports  조선일보
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s economic growth rate in the third quarter significantly surpassed expectations for the third consecutive quarter, driven by sustained increases in semiconductor exports amid the U.S.-led AI (artificial intelligence) boom. The Bank of Korea announced on the 27th that the economy grew by 1.0% quarter-on-quarter in its “Third Quarter Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP)” report. This figure is more than three times the central bank’s August forecast of 0.3%. Year-on-year growth reached 3.4%, also exceeding the projected 2.6%. If this momentum continues through year-end, annual growth could approach 4%, far surpassing the Bank of Korea’s forecast of 3.3%. Lee Dong-won, head of the Bank of Korea’s Economic Statistics Division 2, stated, “If fourth-quarter growth remains at the current level, annual growth would reach approximately 3.9%. A quarter-on-quarter growth rate of 1.4% or higher would enable annual growth of 4%.”
Similar to the first and second quarters, exports grew by 2.3% quarter-on-quarter, led by semiconductors and other IT items, marking a higher increase than the second quarter’s 1.3%. Year-on-year export growth was 8.6%, slightly lower than the second quarter’s 8.9%. Equipment investment increased by 4.1% quarter-on-quarter and 9.4% year-on-year, driven by rising semiconductor facility investments. Lee Dong-won explained, “Semiconductors accounted for roughly half of the overall growth.”
Despite strong export-driven growth, private consumption declined by 0.2% quarter-on-quarter, marking the first decrease since the fourth quarter of 2022, during the COVID-19 pandemic. In the second quarter, private consumption had risen by 0.4% due to improved consumer sentiment from a stock market rally and increased home appliance purchases from Samsung Electronics’ gift certificate redemption event. However, these effects dissipated in the third quarter. Lee Dong-won noted, “Declines in financial service consumption due to reduced stock trading volumes and delayed car deliveries from automaker strikes contributed to the drop. Private consumption is expected to rebound in the fourth quarter due to semiconductor company dividends and performance-based bonuses in early 2024, which will boost household income.”
The Bank of Korea explained, “Consumption of goods like passenger vehicles and home appliances, as well as services such as finance and dining, all decreased.” Year-on-year private consumption growth was 1.1%. Government consumption increased by 1.9% quarter-on-quarter and 2.6% year-on-year, driven by higher spending on goods, health insurance benefits, and other expenses.
The third-quarter real gross domestic income (GDI), which reflects export prices, rose by 3.4% quarter-on-quarter as AI-driven demand surged, pushing semiconductor prices higher. While this was a slight decline from the previous quarter’s 3.7%, it remained over three times the GDP growth rate. Year-on-year GDI growth reached 18.8%, the highest since the fourth quarter of 1977, up from the previous quarter.
While GDP measures domestic production, GDI is calculated by adjusting export prices relative to import prices. Despite rising oil import costs due to the Middle East conflict, semiconductor export prices increased more sharply, sustaining high GDI growth. The year-on-year GDI growth rate exceeded the GDP growth rate by 15.4 percentage points, marking the third consecutive quarter of record-breaking gaps.
With inflation persistently above the Bank of Korea’s 2% target and strong growth continuing into the third quarter, the likelihood of additional interest rate hikes before year-end has increased. The central bank paused its rate hikes on the 22nd after raising rates twice in July and August. Governor Shin Hyun-song views the semiconductor-driven growth as a demand-side inflationary factor. At a post-meeting press conference, he stated, “Given that growth and inflation trends are stronger than August projections, maintaining the current tight monetary policy stance is necessary.” The final Monetary Policy Board meeting of the year is scheduled for November 26.

China’s expanding semiconductor industry is fuelling anxiety in South Korea, where a new report from PwC has warned local chipmakers to defend profitability as Chinese rivals scale up production and strengthen market share.
Samil PwC, the South Korean member firm of the global consultancy, said in a report made public on Monday that Chinese competition would likely heat up first in the areas of conventional memory, mature-node manufacturing, and packaging and testing.
To stay ahead, Samil PwC urged South Korean semiconductor companies to sharpen cost competitiveness in commodity memory while doubling down on cutting-edge sectors such as advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which are used alongside AI processors in a stacked configuration.

articles.title: From 24 GPUs to 4: Three South Korean Startups Shaking Up the AI Chip Game - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: From 24 GPUs to 4: Three South Korean Startups Shaking Up the AI Chip Game  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
As artificial intelligence (AI) computing costs emerge as corporate America's biggest burden, South Korean startups that are shaking up the market along a different axis from the chip performance race are drawing attention. The protagonists are Nota, Lablup and MangoBoost, which respectively handle model lightweighting, graphics processing unit (GPU) resource allocation and data center infrastructure efficiency.
The most eye-catching result came from Nota. The company cut the number of Nvidia B300 GPUs needed to run Alibaba's 2.4-trillion-parameter Qwen 3.8 model from 24 to four. It also reduced H100 GPU usage on Upstage's Solar Open 2 from eight to two. The gains come from combining quantization, which lowers a model's computational precision, with pruning, which cuts away low-importance parts. At an International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) competition, it placed in the top ranks by boosting the inference speed of the 4-billion-parameter Qwen 3.5 model roughly sevenfold on a single Nvidia A10G GPU.
Lablup handles the area of sharing GPUs among multiple users. Its Backend.AI platform pools scattered GPUs into a single resource and automatically allocates as much as each task needs. It manages simultaneous training and inference by multiple users so that jobs do not collide, allowing companies to raise utilization rates without buying additional equipment. The company has also joined DGX Ready, Nvidia's technology partner program.
MangoBoost raises efficiency at the level of the entire data center. Building on more than a decade of data processing unit (DPU) research by Seoul National University researchers, it supplies the GPU server Alfonso, the storage server Caesar and the inference software LLM Boost as a package. Its strength is optimizing hardware and software simultaneously without being tied to a specific semiconductor vendor, and it is also working with AMD.
Some ask whether the spread of efficiency technology will reduce semiconductor demand. The industry's judgment leans the opposite way. The argument is that as the cost of using AI falls, services and users will multiply and total computing volume may actually grow. Global consulting firm McKinsey projected that about 60% of total AI computing demand in 2030 will come from inference. Market research firm TrendForce analyzed that an efficient AI model can process up to six times as many tokens on the same accelerator configuration as an existing large model.
SK Hynix also said in its second-quarter earnings announcement that "the emergence of high-efficiency AI models will not necessarily lead to a reduction in AI infrastructure investment." Its judgment is that the AI market itself grows because more users can use a wider variety of services on the same infrastructure. Because memory bandwidth, which supplies data quickly during inference, remains a bottleneck, the importance of high-performance, high-capacity memory is preserved even as GPU computing performance rises.
This trend could lead memory makers to expand their product lines. Demand need not stay confined to high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for training but can broaden to server DRAM, low-power memory and enterprise solid-state drives (eSSD). As agentic AI and on-device AI spread, memory demand for smartphones, PCs, cars and robots is also expected to grow.
A change in how memory itself is designed is another variable. When the custom HBM market — customer-tailored HBM — opens in earnest next year, the scope of competition for memory makers shifts from storage capacity and speed to the performance and power efficiency of the entire AI system. If HBM is likened to an apartment building, the upper floors are the space that stores data, and the approach is to put customer-requested functions into the "base die" — the first floor that exchanges data with external AI chips. Nvidia's NVHBM, unveiled in August, centers on moving the memory control circuitry found in existing AI accelerators into the base die.
Ahn Hyun, head of development at SK Hynix and a president of the company, said in a keynote speech at the SEDEX semiconductor exhibition on the 14th that "standard HBM and custom HBM will coexist, but over the long term the custom trend will expand further." Because custom HBM reflects each customer's design requirements, its unit price is higher than standard products, making it an opportunity for memory makers to widen a high-value-added market.
The more customized design expands, however, the greater the tension over who leads design and production. Because the space for customer-specific circuitry must be decided jointly, memory makers must implement their own circuitry in a smaller area. It is in the same context that a plan is being discussed to have the base die that Samsung Electronics has produced in its own foundry made instead at rival TSMC, in line with Nvidia's requirements. If other AI chip developers such as AMD and Broadcom later demand TSMC processes as well, a structure could spread in which memory makers secure orders but leave production of core components to outside parties. That is why some argue that the mix of standard and custom products must be adjusted in light of per-customer profitability and dependence on specific foundries.
In the end, the competitive axis of the semiconductor market is shifting from the performance of a single chip to an optimization ecosystem spanning models, hardware and infrastructure. As the view spreads that simply adding more high-performance GPUs cannot keep up with surging computing demand and cost burdens, technology that bridges the gap between models and hardware is taking shape as an independent industry. The question is whether, while chipmakers and model developers focus on the performance race, the technology of the South Korean startups connecting the two can be evaluated in the global market as an alternative.

articles.title: Japan, South Korea stocks fall as Asian shares make cautious start ahead of earnings - The Business Times
articles.summary: Japan, South Korea stocks fall as Asian shares make cautious start ahead of earnings  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eases 0.1%
[SYDNEY] Share markets got off to a cautious start on Monday (Oct 26) as oil eased from six-month highs ahead of a week packed with central bank meetings and company earnings that will further test investor confidence in the artificial intelligence boom.
Brent oil slipped 1 per cent to US$115.48 amid reports Qatari mediators were in Teheran on Sunday as part of an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the US.
Brent futures jumped 6.2 per cent last week to their highest weekly close since mid-2022 as Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over energy supplies. US crude futures fell 1.1 per cent to US$102.08 a barrel.
Japan’s Nikkei dipped 0.8 per cent, after losing 4 per cent last week, while South Korea fell 0.4 per cent, having shed almost 19 per cent so far in October. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.1 per cent.
The inflationary pulse from oil is likely to alarm all the central banks meeting this week, with hikes seen as just a matter of time even if some hold for now.
“The main message from global central banks grappling with 2026’s macroeconomic surprises is that a relatively shallow rate hike cycle is underway,” said Bruce Kasman, global head of economics at JPMorgan.
“G3 central banks are likely to remain on hold, but Canada should start its tightening cycle and first moves are expected from the UK and Sweden (in September).”
New Zealand’s central bank is widely expected to raise rates on Wednesday. Markets assume the US Federal Reserve will stand pat, but imply an 80 per cent chance it will pull the trigger in December. Much the same is priced in for the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank.
A key reading on US core inflation should show cost pressures remained elevated at 3.1 per cent in September, while the economy is forecast to have grown at a brisk 3.2 per cent annualised pace thanks in part to furious spending on data centres.
“The Fed is set to skip raising rates at its October meeting but is likely to deliver a second hike in December,” analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a note.
“The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran,” they added.
“The more extreme and long-lasting the energy shock becomes, the more Fed participants will worry that inflationary pressures could broaden.”
Hyperscalers to test AI hype
On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures both edged up 0.2 per cent. In Europe, Eurostoxx 50 futures firmed 0.2 per cent, while DAX futures gained 0.1 per cent.
Earnings highlights will include the hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, among one-third of S&P 500 companies reporting. Results from Intel and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade.
Consensus on Microsoft is for US$90.6 billion of revenue and an adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of US$4.73, with Amazon at US$202 billion of revenue and EPS around US$1.97. Alphabet revenue is seen at US$128 billion and EPS of US$3.00.
Equity valuations have been tested by higher bond yields, though Treasuries did manage a rally last week before running into renewed selling on Friday.
Yields on 10-year Treasuries were at 5 per cent, but off a peak of 5.36 per cent hit early in October.
In currency markets, the Japanese yen retained its safe-haven appeal at 157.00 per US dollar, having gained around 0.8 per cent last week.
The euro held steady at US$1.1204 as political unrest in France kept investors wary, though the country did escape a credit downgrade last week.
Sterling held at US$1.3346 with Britain’s new finance minister, John Healey, set to deliver his first budget on Wednesday against a backdrop of rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the Iran war.
The Brazilian real was yet to trade in Asia as Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, the country’s electoral court said.
In commodity markets, non-interest bearing gold was a fraction firmer at US$4,001 an ounce, having fallen more than 4 per cent last week. REUTERS

The growth in July-September accelerated from 0.6 percent in the previous quarter and surpassed the central bank’s August forecast of 0.3 percent. On a year-on-year basis, the economy expanded 3.4 percent.
South Korea’s export performance was driven by booming global demand for semiconductors amid the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Exports reached a record $120.9 billion in September, up 83.5 percent from a year earlier, with semiconductor shipments exceeding $60 billion.
Facility investment rose 4.1 percent from the previous quarter, while construction investment increased 0.7 percent. Government spending also advanced 1.9 percent. However, private consumption declined 0.2 percent amid stock market weakness and sluggish automobile sales affected by strikes at major automakers.
The BOK said South Korea’s economy grew a cumulative 3.6 percent during the first three quarters of 2026.
“If the economy maintains the on-quarter growth pace in the fourth quarter, GDP will likely grow 3.6 percent for the full year,” said Lee Dong-won of the BOK’s statistics department.
The central bank may revise its August full-year growth forecast of 3.3 percent upward, with updated projections scheduled for release next month.

articles.title: Korea's Wealthiest Investors Dump Samsung, SK hynix for Leveraged Chip ETFs - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Korea's Wealthiest Investors Dump Samsung, SK hynix for Leveraged Chip ETFs  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
Investors with more than 3 billion won ($2.1 million) in financial assets are shifting how they bet on semiconductors as South Korea's stock market turns more volatile. They are cutting direct holdings in large-cap chip stocks and concentrating instead on exchange-traded funds that track gains in the sector or the broader market.
The Seoul Economic Daily commissioned a major brokerage to analyze the five largest net purchases and net sales by about 7,900 high-net-worth investors between the 1st and the 20th of this month, and compared them with the same period last month. The results showed a clear shift in how these investors approach the chip sector.
Their largest net purchase this month was KODEX Semiconductor Leverage, with 33.2 billion won in net buying. The fund is a high-risk product that tracks twice the daily return of a semiconductor index. That marks a reversal from last month, when their net buying was concentrated in individual large-cap chip-related stocks such as Samsung Electronics preferred shares (59.6 billion won) and Samsung Electro-Mechanics (19.9 billion won).
Analysts read the shift as a move toward betting on a broad sector rally through ETFs rather than buying large-cap stocks directly. Indeed, the investors sold heavily in Samsung Electronics and SK hynix in both months, with net sales of 55.9 billion won and 92.4 billion won, respectively, in October alone. Among individual stocks, only SK Square (28.6 billion won) and Samsung SDI (12.5 billion won) saw net buying. Three of the five most-bought products this month were ETFs. Last month, all five were individual stocks: Samsung Electronics preferred shares, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Samsung SDI (11.7 billion won), Doosan Enerbility (8.2 billion won) and Doosan Fuel Cell (7.7 billion won).
Another notable trend is a wager on a rise in the overall market. This month the investors net bought 22.5 billion won of KODEX Leverage, which tracks twice the daily return of the KOSPI 200 index, and 10.5 billion won of KODEX 200. By contrast, they net sold 8 billion won of KODEX 200 Futures Inverse 2X, which gains when the index falls. Among index-linked products, they trimmed bearish positions and concentrated buying on bullish ones with a longer-term view.
An official at a major brokerage said the defining feature this month is that high-net-worth investors are reducing direct exposure to large-cap chip stocks while still placing weight on the prospect of gains in the sector and the market as a whole.

articles.title: Bank of Korea warns country's chip exports could fall by up to $100 billion if AI spending slows - Business Recorder
articles.summary: Bank of Korea warns country's chip exports could fall by up to $100 billion if AI spending slows  Business Recorder
articles.full_text:
- The assessment underscores growing anxiety over South Korea's heavy reliance on chips, which account for roughly half of its exports
A slowdown in US tech AI spending could slash South Korea's chip exports by up to $100 billion, significantly impacting its GDP and current account.
- Potential $50B-$100B decline in South Korea's chip exports.
- Impact on South Korea's GDP growth and current account surplus.
- Uncertainty in AI demand and memory chip business cycle.
SEOUL: South Korea’s semiconductor exports could fall by $50 billion to $100 billion compared with earlier forecasts if capital spending on artificial intelligence by major US technology firms slows next year, according to central bank data.
In a written response submitted to lawmaker Ahn Do-geol, the Bank of Korea (BOK) modelled a “pessimistic scenario” to assess the economic fallout if US tech giants curb their aggressive infrastructure outlays.
Under the scenario, a sudden export shortfall would shave approximately 0.4 percentage point off South Korea’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate next year, by driving the country’s current account surplus well below the central bank’s initial projection of $430 billion for 2027.
The scenario assumed a 10% decline in Korean semiconductor unit prices.
The assessment underscores growing anxiety over South Korea’s heavy reliance on chips, which account for roughly half of its exports.
The report said combined capital expenditure by five major US technology firms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle, has been growing rapidly, from $40 billion last year to an estimated $80 billion this year, and is projected to reach $110 billion next year.
However, the BOK cautioned that considerable uncertainty remains over the trajectory of AI demand and the broader memory chip business cycle.

articles.full_text:
South Korean semiconductor materials, components and equipment stocks surged across the board in early trading on the 27th, as the initial public offering push by U.S. artificial intelligence firm Anthropic revived investor appetite for technology shares. Buying spread quickly from large-cap chipmakers such as Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK hynix (000660.KS) to printed circuit board makers, front-end equipment suppliers and back-end packaging firms.
Simmtech traded at 123,000 won, up 14.63% from the previous session, as of 9:28 a.m., according to the Korea Exchange. Daeduck Electronics (353200.KS) rose 12.28% to 134,400 won, while Korea Circuit gained 10.84% to 73,600 won. Analysts said investor sentiment toward chip stocks had carried over to makers of high-specification PCBs.
Chip equipment makers also advanced. Jusung Engineering (036930.KS) rose 8.29% to 181,500 won and Wonik IPS (240810.KS) traded 6.49% higher at 95,200 won. HPSP gained 4.79%. Among test equipment makers, Exicon jumped 17.56% and Hanyang Digitech soared 15.00%. New Power Plasma rose 10.36%.
Back-end and component stocks drew buying as well. Hana Micron (067310.KS) rose 7.42% to 36,200 won and ISC (095340.KS) gained 5.90% to 148,900 won. Hanmi Semiconductor (042700.KS) climbed 5.87% to 194,800 won. With the rally broadening across the supply chain, some small- and mid-cap names posted double-digit percentage gains.
Large-cap chipmakers set off the advance. SK hynix traded at 1.365 million won, up 7.06%, and Samsung Electronics rose 5.40% to 224,500 won. SK Square (402340.KS), which holds a stake in SK hynix, jumped 10.40%.
On Wall Street overnight, news that Anthropic had formalized its listing process rekindled sentiment toward AI investment. With a valuation of as much as $2 trillion and a potential fundraising of $100 billion under discussion, confirmation of the company's steep revenue growth eased some concerns about the durability of AI infrastructure spending. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 2.82%, with Micron, Nvidia and Broadcom all gaining.
Still, it remains to be tested whether expanded AI investment translates into actual profit and cash flow. Spending burdens are mounting, with some big technology companies including Meta turning to large-scale external fundraising. For now, a recovery in expectations for AI demand is lifting share prices from large-cap chipmakers to their suppliers, but whether the rebound continues will hinge on big technology earnings and their ability to generate cash.
"In the short term this is positive for South Korean memory chips, but for investment expansion to continue, funding conditions and the timing of cash recovery need to support it," said Yang Hyun-kyung, an analyst at iM Securities.

articles.full_text:
South Korea's economy grew 1.0% in the third quarter, far exceeding the Bank of Korea's forecast, as strong semiconductor exports and facility investment combined with higher government spending. Private consumption, however, posted its weakest performance in four and a half years, signaling that growth driven by exports and investment has yet to spread to domestic demand.
Real gross domestic product rose 1.0% from the previous quarter, according to advance estimates for the third quarter of 2026 released by the central bank on the 27th. The figure was 0.7 percentage points above the 0.3% projection the bank issued in August. Growth from a year earlier came in at 3.4%, also topping the 2.6% forecast made at the time.
With third-quarter growth well ahead of expectations, the central bank is now more likely to raise its 3.3% full-year growth forecast.
The rebound was led by exports and facility investment, centered on semiconductors. Exports rose 2.3% from the previous quarter, driven by chips as well as machinery and electrical equipment. Facility investment climbed 4.1% as spending on machinery, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment, increased. Manufacturing grew 2.0%, led by computers, electronic and optical devices and machinery and equipment, lifting overall growth by 0.6 percentage points.
Private consumption, by contrast, fell 0.2% from the previous quarter, the weakest reading since the first quarter of 2022, when it dropped 1.0%. Spending declined not only on goods such as passenger cars and home appliances but also on services including finance and dining. Growth in the service sector slowed to 0.2% from 1.0% in the previous quarter.
Government spending partly offset the weakness in private consumption. Government consumption rose 1.9% as outlays on goods and health insurance benefits increased. As a result, the public sector's contribution to growth swung to 0.8 percentage points from minus 0.5 percentage points in the previous quarter. The private sector's contribution fell to 0.2 percentage points from 1.1 percentage points, with private consumption subtracting 0.1 percentage point.
The consumption trend echoes concerns raised in a central bank report on the outlook for a recovery in private consumption, released on the 22nd. The bank found that despite the semiconductor boom, the pickup in spending has been concentrated in certain product categories and income groups, and that its momentum weakened in the third quarter.
Greater stock market volatility is also seen as a variable for consumer spending. Falling share prices erode the value of financial assets such as equities, which can squeeze household spending capacity. Households may also cut back in response to shrinking assets or delay purchases in anticipation of economic uncertainty.
Market analysts say the growth rebound should be assessed alongside domestic demand. In a survey of 22 market experts on the central bank's rate decision, conducted by Seoul Economic Daily from the 15th to the 19th, Yoon Yeo-sam, a research fellow at Meritz Securities, said third-quarter growth could reach the 1% range but stressed the need to examine the impact on domestic demand and vulnerable groups.
Meanwhile, real gross domestic income, a measure of the economy's purchasing power, rose 3.4% from the previous quarter and surged 18.8% from a year earlier. The year-on-year gain was the largest since the fourth quarter of 1977.

articles.title: North Korean Dictator Kim Jong-un Makes Surprise China Visit - Breitbart
articles.summary: North Korean Dictator Kim Jong-un Makes Surprise China Visit  Breitbart
articles.full_text:
Kim reportedly crossed the New Yalu River Bridge on Saturday and returned to North Korea the same way after spending the day in China’s border city of Dandong, where he visited a memorial to China’s involvement in the Korean War (1950-1953) and met with a senior Chinese Communist Party official Wang Huning.
The New Yalu River Bridge project was launched in 2010 as a symbol of cooperation and friendship between North Korea and China, financed primarily by China. The four-lane, three-kilometer bridge was actually completed 12 years ago, linking Dandong with the North Korean city of Sinuiju, but its opening was delayed indefinitely due to incomplete roads and other infrastructure on the North Korean side.
One of the major reasons for North Korea’s tardy completion of the Sinuiju side of the bridge was a deterioration of the relationship between North Korea and China. This was accompanied by an even sharper deterioration in Kim Jong-un’s relationship with his uncle, Jang Song-thaek, who championed a closer relationship with China and wanted to emulate some features of the Chinese Communist government in North Korea.
Kim had Jang executed in 2013 and the New Yalu River Bridge project faltered soon afterward. Writing for UPI on Monday, North Korean defector and former top economic official Ri Jong-ho referred to the span from Dandong to Sinuiju as “Jang Song-thaek’s bridge” and suggested Beijing forced Kim to drive across it on Saturday, just a few days after it finally opened.
Ri said Beijing probably took North Korea’s opening of a new bridge to Russia last month as an “insult,” and prodded Kim to finally open the “neglected” New Yalu River Bridge, symbolically opening a gateway between North Korea and China that Kim would rather have kept closed.
“Protocol tells you who holds the higher rank. Kim did not go as far as Beijing. He spent the day in Dandong and went home without meeting Xi. The man who received him was not a head of state but Wang Huning, the Party’s No. 4,” Ri pointed out.
Furthermore, Kim sat for a photo with Wang that would look humiliating to North Korean eyes, because it presented China’s number four man as an equal of the supposedly sacred North Korean dictator. There was also some symbolic messaging in Kim’s visit to the Dandong war memorial, which presents China’s contribution to the war as much more decisive than North Korea’s propaganda materials and museums do.
The date of Kim’s visit, October 25, was the date of China’s first major battlefield victory in the Korean War in 1950.
Chinese state media carried a speech from Kim at the end of his brief visit, in which he pledged that Pyongyang “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries.”
Kim said North Korea would “forever remember the glorious years of fighting alongside the Chinese people,” and would continue expressing “generational gratitude to the Chinese people who helped our revolution with blood.”
Daily NK noted that some of that long-incomplete infrastructure on the North Korean side of the New Yalu River Bridge still isn’t working well, while customs inspections on the Chinese side can get a bit awkward:
Since the formal opening, drivers have waited in their trucks for more than three hours at a time, a source in China told Daily NK on Wednesday. Chinese customs inspections are taking far longer than expected, and North Korean customs has also struggled to keep vehicles moving.
At times, lines of trucks waiting for clearance have stretched a third of the way across the bridge. The span runs roughly 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) across the Yalu River.
According to the source, Chinese customs officers are checking shipments closely for goods banned under UN Security Council sanctions. Since 2006, the council has passed a series of resolutions in response to Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile tests. These measures restrict trade in items ranging from machinery and vehicles to coal, textiles and seafood.
Bureaucratic fumbling on both sides of the bridge hinted that the decision to finally open it for commercial traffic, after 12 years of delays, came as a surprise to both Chinese and North Korean customs officials.
There is another, much smaller, bridge linking Sinuiju with Dandong, a single-lane span called the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, built by the Imperial Japanese Army during its occupation of Korea and parts of China during World War 2. In addition to carrying less historical baggage, the New Yalu River Bridge will greatly increase the amount of road cargo that can be shipped across the Chinese border.
When the new bridge opened on October 15, the BBC predicted it would not lead to a “sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border” because China remains reluctant to violate U.N. sanctions on North Korea, and North Korea is worried about a flood of Chinese goods overwhelming its consumer markets.
In his post for UPI, Ri Jong-ho noted that Kim Jong-un brought his sister Kim Yo-jong, his foreign minister, and some senior party secretaries with him to Dandong, but only one “economic official of note,” First Vice Premier Kim Tok-hun.
“This was a delegation for a political ceremony, not one sent to negotiate trade and economic opening,” Ri concluded.
Meanwhile, tensions between North and South Korea continued running high over the weekend. South Korean observers reported seeing armored vehicles and howitzers moving along the North Korean side of the demilitarized zone (DMZ), the buffer region around the border between the two Koreas.
The howitzers were seemingly deployed to protect squads of North Korean soldiers while they constructed fences inside the DMZ. Security analysts said it was highly unusual for North Korea to move its self-propelled artillery close to the border in a show of force.
On Sunday, North Korea state media reported that the Kim regime sent a letter to the United Nations that accused South Korea of exploiting a landmine detonation on September 21 to ratchet up tensions and interfere with North Korea’s ability to fortify its border.
The landmine that exploded in September injured three South Korean soldiers who were patrolling their side of the DMZ. In its letter to the U.N., North Korea accused South Korea of fabricating the incident as a pretext for hostilities, and further accused South Korean forces of illegally firing at North Korean personnel.

articles.title: Ted Sarandos: Netflix Marks 10 Years in South Korea - The Chenab Times
articles.summary: Ted Sarandos: Netflix Marks 10 Years in South Korea  The Chenab Times
articles.full_text:
Netflix co-chief executive Ted Sarandos marked a significant milestone for the streaming giant in South Korea, attending an event in Seoul to commemorate the company’s ten-year presence in the country. The celebration occurred as Netflix faces ongoing scrutiny in the United States over various business practices.
The Chenab Times has learned that Sarandos, typically a key figure in the company’s global expansion strategies, was a visible presence at the anniversary event. South Korea has become a crucial market for Netflix, particularly as a launchpad for globally successful Korean-language content. The streamer has leveraged this success to build a substantial subscriber base and production infrastructure within the nation.
During his visit, Sarandos highlighted the impact of Korean content on the global entertainment landscape. South Korea has been instrumental in Netflix’s international growth, notably with the phenomenal success of series like "Squid Game," "Kingdom," and "K-pop Demon Hunters." These productions have not only garnered massive viewership worldwide but have also elevated the global profile of Korean culture and entertainment.
The ten-year anniversary underscores Netflix’s sustained investment in the South Korean market. The company has cultivated strong relationships with local creators, actors, and production houses, fostering an environment that allows for the development of distinctive and compelling narratives. This collaborative approach has been a cornerstone of Netflix’s strategy in building its content library and brand presence.
Sarandos’s appearance in Seoul comes at a time when Netflix’s operations and strategies are under intense examination in its home market. The streaming giant has been navigating challenges including increased competition, evolving subscriber behaviors, and regulatory discussions in the United States. Despite these domestic pressures, the company’s commitment to international markets like South Korea remains a vital component of its long-term growth plan.
South Korea was among the first countries in Asia where Netflix established a significant presence, signaling its early recognition of the region’s potential. The streamer’s journey in the country has been characterized by a steady expansion of its content offerings, investment in local production facilities, and a strategic approach to understanding and catering to regional tastes.
The success of Korean original series has provided Netflix with a unique competitive advantage, allowing it to tap into a diverse global audience increasingly interested in non-English language content. This trend has been further amplified by the rise of K-culture, encompassing music, film, and television, which has cultivated a dedicated international following.
The anniversary event in Seoul served as a platform for Netflix to reiterate its commitment to the Korean market, emphasizing its role as a partner in the continued growth of the country’s creative industries. It also provided an opportunity for Sarandos to engage with local stakeholders and discuss future collaborations and content strategies.

articles.title: K-beauty, chips push Korean SME exports to Q3 record - Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.summary: K-beauty, chips push Korean SME exports to Q3 record  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
Korean small businesses posted a record $33.4 billion in third quarter exports as cosmetics and semiconductor demand surged, with the United States overtaking China as their top market.
Beauty influencers and local shoppers turn out for the opening of the "Olive Young K-Beauty Edit" at Sephora's Times Square store in New York on Aug. 20.CJ OLIVE YOUNG
Korean small- and medium-sized enterprises (SME) exported a third quarter record of $33.4 billion as overseas demand for K-beauty products and semiconductors surged.
The July-to-September total was up 8.8 percent from a year earlier, the Ministry of SMEs and Startups said Monday in its quarterly report on SME export trends.
Cumulative exports for the first nine months rose 9.5 percent on year to $96.5 billion. The number of SMEs that exported goods rose 1.6 percent to 90,765, also the most on record.
Cosmetics led the growth. Cosmetics exports in the third quarter rose 28.6 percent on year to $2.79 billion, while cosmetics exports for the first nine months climbed 26.4 percent to $7.65 billion. Each figure was a third quarter record.
Independent brands built name recognition on online platforms such as Amazon and TikTok Shop before expanding into major North American retail chains. Their online success and expansion into physical stores helped drive export growth.
K-beauty exporters are also reaching more markets. Third quarter cosmetics exports rose 33.1 percent to North America and 58.6 percent to Europe. Shipments to Latin America, an emerging market, surged 141.3 percent.
The number of SMEs exporting cosmetics rose 6.3 percent on year to 9,469 in the first nine months. Cosmetics accounted for 75.3 percent of the $470 million that SMEs exported through online channels in the third quarter.
Semiconductor exports jumped 68.8 percent to $1.39 billion in the third quarter amid a boom in the AI market. Chipmaking equipment exports grew 38.3 percent to $1.14 billion. Both figures were third quarter records.
Petroleum product exports rose 29.3 percent to $660 million, partly due to higher global oil prices.
Automobile exports, by contrast, fell 42.4 percent to $1.51 billion over the same period. Shipments to Russia and Central Asia declined partly because of a Russian tax on imported used cars, while instability in the Middle East further hurt exports. A 66.6 percent plunge in automobile exports to the United Arab Emirates made the overall decline steeper.
The United States overtook China as the largest destination for SME exports in the third quarter. Exports to the United States rose 19.6 percent on year to $5.73 billion during the period.
Cosmetics exports to the United States grew as distribution networks for K-beauty products expanded in the country. Exports of rechargeable batteries and related materials also increased.
"Despite an unstable external environment, SME exports are making gains in major markets such as the United States and emerging markets such as Latin America," Shim Jae-yoon, director-general for global growth policy at the ministry, said. "We will strengthen support through export vouchers and programs that help large companies and SMEs expand overseas together."

articles.title: Inside Henkel's Korean factory making adhesives for AI chips - The Korea Herald
articles.summary: Inside Henkel's Korean factory making adhesives for AI chips  The Korea Herald
articles.full_text:
German chemicals giant strengthens Korean semiconductor materials hub as AI drives demand for advanced packaging, with new R&D center planned for 2027
SONGDO, Incheon — Inside a tightly controlled factory in Songdo, German chemicals giant Henkel is producing a critical but often overlooked ingredient in AI chips: semiconductor adhesives.
Workers in cleanroom suits operate mixing equipment under strict temperature and humidity controls. Some rooms glow yellow, with ultraviolet light filtered out to prevent unwanted chemical reactions.
The materials produced here help hold chips together, protect delicate connections and dissipate heat — increasingly demanding tasks as AI requires more powerful processors and complex semiconductor packaging.
For Henkel, the Songdo plant is a strategic foothold in South Korea's semiconductor industry, home to memory giants Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, and a growing base for supplying chipmaking materials across Asia and beyond.
Completed in 2022 following a roughly 35 million euro ($39.2 million) investment, the 10,144-square-meter facility is the only one of Henkel's four Korean factories to produce semiconductor adhesives. It also represents the company's largest single investment in Korea, excluding acquisitions.
"This is one of the major, important production sites for the semiconductor industry for advanced packaging," said Hendrik Kohleick, Henkel's regional president for Asia-Pacific operations.
The plant has annual semiconductor adhesive production capacity of up to 250 metric tons. Its broader manufacturing portfolio spans more than 500 adhesive solutions for semiconductor packaging, electronic components and device assembly, the company said.
Henkel is also expanding its research presence in Korea. Kohleick said the company planned to open a new technical center, expanding its existing R&D operations in Seoul's Gasan Digital Complex, to meet growing demand for advanced adhesives as chipmakers pursue greater integration and confront increasingly difficult thermal management challenges.
The center is tentatively scheduled to open in March 2027 and will work closely with the Songdo production site, he added.
As chipmakers pack more computing power into increasingly complex packages, they must contend with heat, mechanical stress and delicate connections between components. Materials used to attach, protect and support those components must meet increasingly demanding specifications.
"Customers are seeking adhesives that flow more readily and can form thinner bonding layers as chips and the spaces between components shrink," said Chang Ho-jun, president and head of Adhesive Technologies at Henkel Korea. Such materials help reduce the space occupied by adhesives within a package, supporting thinner designs, he added.
For Henkel, a production base in Korea puts it close to major semiconductor manufacturers as they develop more advanced chips and packaging technologies.
"Since entering the Korean market, Henkel has built a solid business foundation over nearly 40 years," said Kim Young-mi, president of Henkel Korea. "With the recent growth of the global AI market and the strength of Korea's semiconductor industry, we expect the Songdo plant's role to become increasingly important."
Inside the factory, production proceeds through seven stages, from inspecting and weighing raw materials to mixing, milling additives, testing finished products and filling syringe-style containers.
The finished adhesives are packaged in piston-operated syringes, with around 100 combinations of syringe barrels and dispensing caps available to accommodate customers' application requirements.
Consistency matters as much as formulation. The facility uses cleanrooms rated at Class 10,000, alongside systems that monitor production and collect process data. Statistical process controls help track variation during manufacturing, according to Henkel.
That infrastructure supports a business in which customers need materials that perform predictably within tightly controlled manufacturing processes. The planned Gasan expansion would add research capacity to support the development and application of those materials.
Songdo's location also helps explain the manufacturing investment.
Incheon International Airport is about 30 minutes away, giving the factory access to overseas customers. Much of its output travels by air, Kim said, adding that competitive cargo rates offered by major Korean airlines helped make Songdo an attractive production base.
The company, which marks its 150th anniversary this year, is familiar to many consumers through brands such as Persil. Adhesive Technologies, however, is a major business in its own right, generating about 10.7 billion euros in sales last year, compared with about 9.8 billion euros for Consumer Brands.
Its semiconductor portfolio includes die-attach materials, which bond chips to supporting surfaces; underfills, which reinforce connections beneath chips; and encapsulants, which protect components.
Henkel says it is expanding that portfolio for AI and high-performance computing, including materials for larger dies and more complex packaging structures. Its recently introduced Loctite Ablestik CDF900 series of thermally conductive die-attach films targets applications including AI, high-performance computing and next-generation communications.
"Songdo will strengthen cooperation with customers as a supply base for advanced semiconductor materials and continue developing long-term partnerships," Kohleick said.

articles.title: Yongin opens semiconductor high school, secures 52-firm hiring pipeline in Korea - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Yongin opens semiconductor high school, secures 52-firm hiring pipeline in Korea - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
Yongin, Gyeonggi Province, will begin accepting applications for first-year students to Yongin Semiconductor High School, the city's first semiconductor-specialized high school opening in March next year. Fifty-two semiconductor corporations have signed hiring-related agreements with the school, allowing 109 students to be employed immediately after graduation.
Yongin said on the 26th that it will accept applications for the 2027 freshman admissions process for Yongin Semiconductor High School from Nov. 3 to 5.
Yongin Semiconductor High School will be built next March on 17,634 square meters at the site of the closed Namgok branch school in Namsa-eup, Cheoin-gu. It will open with two departments—semiconductor manufacturing and semiconductor equipment—across 24 classes with 16 students per class.
Starting in March 2028, it will be converted into a Meister high school and operated as Yongin Semiconductor Meister High School (tentative name). Upon conversion, it will run two departments: "semiconductor manufacturing process," which teaches the full flow and practical skills across the eight major semiconductor processes, and "semiconductor equipment," specialized in equipment maintenance, automation control, and facility operation.
Yongin Semiconductor High School has been a key initiative pursued by the city administration since the eighth popular election. Mayor Lee Sang-il has met with education authorities since taking office in July 2022, emphasizing the need to establish a semiconductor Meister high school. After these efforts, in 2024 the Ministry of Education approved the designation of a semiconductor-specialized high school. Construction of Yongin Semiconductor High School began in December last year, and it was designated a Meister high school in June this year.
Alongside preparations to establish the semiconductor high school, Yongin has also prepared support measures. It signed business agreements with semiconductor-related corporations such as Samsung Electronics(005930), SK hynix(000660), and SurplusGLOBAL to develop curricula for talent cultivation, provide teacher job-skill guidance, and support student training. To ensure graduates can work on site immediately, the city secured agreements with a total of 52 semiconductor corporations and obtained hiring commitments for 109 graduates.
The city is also working with local universities to cultivate semiconductor talent. It signed business agreements with six universities that operate semiconductor-related departments—Kangnam University, Kyunghee University, Dankook University, Myongji University, Yongin Arts and Science University, and Hankuk University of Foreign Studies—to form the "Yongin City industry-academia consultative body for cultivating semiconductor talent." The consultative body has so far held five regular meetings to discuss sharing semiconductor education resources, cooperation with the Meister high school, and jointly promoting integrated training for new employees at local corporations.
Mayor Lee Sang-il said, "As Yongin, where semiconductors were first produced in Korea in 1983, grows into a global hub of the semiconductor industry, fostering and developing semiconductor-related talent is also important," adding, "the establishment and opening of Yongin Semiconductor High School means that the cultivation of semiconductor talent is in full swing in Yongin."

articles.title: North Korea and Ukraine pose linked security challenge: Belgian minister - Aju Press
articles.summary: North Korea and Ukraine pose linked security challenge: Belgian minister  Aju Press
articles.full_text:
SEOUL, October 26 (AJP) - North Korea’s deployment of troops and weapons to support Russia’s war in Ukraine has made Pyongyang a security threat to Europe as well as South Korea, Belgian Deputy Prime Minister Maxime Prévot said.
“We are also deeply concerned by North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs, as well as its growing military cooperation with Russia. Developments on the Korean Peninsula and the war in Ukraine are no longer separate security questions. They are increasingly connected,” Prévot, who doubles as foreign minister, said in a written interview with AJP.
The connection is increasingly shaping European policy toward Pyongyang.
On Oct. 12, the Council of the European Union imposed sanctions on three individuals and four entities linked to North Korea’s weapons programs and sanctions evasion. The measures targeted activities supporting its cooperation with Russia, including North Korean workers, commercial and industrial ties and an “arms-for-oil” trade.
The same day, North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the East Sea, with at least one traveling more than 900 kilometers, according to South Korea’s military.
Pyongyang’s supply of ammunition, missiles and troops to Russia has made the relationship a shared concern for Seoul and European capitals.
The response requires stronger defense capabilities and closer partnerships extending beyond conventional military cooperation.
“South Korea is an important partner in this respect. Your technological expertise, defence industry, battery production and semiconductor capabilities offer significant opportunities for closer collaboration with Europe,” he said.
President Lee Jae Myung’s June summit with EU leaders in Brussels underscored that convergence, with both sides advancing cooperation in defense, security, digital technologies and economic resilience.
Prévot pointed to the Port of Antwerp-Bruges and energy and communications infrastructure in the North Sea as assets whose protection has become central to European security. Ports, electricity grids, digital networks and undersea cables require industrial capacity as well as military protection, he argued.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has exposed Europe’s dependence on external energy supplies and gaps in its defenses. But greater European strategic autonomy, he said, should strengthen its alliances.
“When I speak about European strategic autonomy, I am not advocating isolation or a Europe that turns away from its allies. I am talking about the ability to make our own decisions, defend our interests and fulfil our responsibilities,” he said.
“NATO remains the cornerstone of our collective defense. A stronger Europe should reinforce that alliance, not compete with it. Europe must assume more responsibility for its own security, and that is also in the interest of our American allies.”
The security connection with South Korea also carries a historical obligation. Belgian troops fought under the United Nations flag during the 1950–53 Korean War, and the country remains involved in the United Nations Command.
Prévot visited the Demilitarized Zone and Joint Security Area during his September 2025 trip to South Korea.
“There is something deeply unsettling about standing in a place where, more than seventy years after the armistice, peace remains unfinished. You are reminded that the absence of fighting is not necessarily the same as peace,” he said.
“Belgium remains involved through the United Nations Command, which contributes to maintaining the armistice. We support the Republic of Korea’s efforts to reduce tensions, prevent escalation and pursue lasting peace on the Peninsula,” he said.
“Belgium cannot determine the future of the Peninsula. That future belongs first and foremost to the Korean people. But we can remain a reliable partner, defend international law, support diplomatic efforts and contribute to international security.”
As South Korea and Belgium mark 125 years of diplomatic relations this year, Prévot sees a broader common interest: protecting the room for internationally connected economies to make their own choices amid intensifying competition among major powers.
“For me, that requires three things. Strong alliances, because neither of us can guarantee our security alone. Diversified partnerships, because excessive dependence can quickly become a vulnerability. And international rules, because without them, smaller countries are exposed to the decisions of the most powerful,” he said.
That approach, he stressed, does not mean keeping equal distance from competing powers.
“This is not about equidistance between competing powers. Belgium is firmly anchored in the European Union and NATO, just as South Korea has its own essential security alliances. We know who our allies are,” he said.
“But loyalty to our allies should never prevent us from developing our own capabilities or building constructive relationships with other partners.”
He also warned that selective application of international law undermines the protections on which countries such as Belgium and South Korea depend.
“Civilians must be protected. Humanitarian assistance must reach those who need it. International humanitarian law must be respected. And borders cannot be changed by force,” he said.
“If we defend these principles only when they are convenient, we should not be surprised when others stop believing in them.”
Defending those principles must still leave room for diplomacy with governments Belgium fundamentally opposes.
“Dialogue is not endorsement. Negotiation is not surrender,” he said.
“The real challenge is to remain faithful to our principles while being sufficiently pragmatic to achieve results. The families waiting for an end to a war need more than expressions of concern. They need us to use every available diplomatic instrument to make a difference.”
The test of cooperation between Belgium and South Korea is whether they can turn their industrial and diplomatic strengths into influence over the rules governing their security.
“The question is not whether Belgium and South Korea can compete with the great powers on their own terms. It is whether we can help shape a world in which every country does not have to,” he said.

articles.summary: Annual growth could reach 3.6% even with zero growth in Q4, with chip boom raising hopes of 4% growth  머니투데이
articles.full_text:
The likelihood that South Korea’s annual economic growth rate for this year will rise to around 3.7% has increased. As the third-quarter economic growth rate significantly exceeded the Bank of Korea’s forecast, annual growth of 3.6% is possible even if growth stalls in the fourth quarter. This would be the highest growth rate in five years since the rebound following the shock of the coronavirus pandemic in 2021 (4.7%).
According to the Bank of Korea on the 27th, the third-quarter real gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate was 1.0%, surpassing the forecast from last August (0.3%) by 0.7 percentage points. This figure can raise the annual growth rate by 0.35 percentage points.
The Bank of Korea raised its forecast for this year’s annual growth rate from 2.6% to 3.3% in August last month. Simply reflecting the effect of the third-quarter outperformance brings the figure to 3.65%. This is the backdrop for suggestions that it may be further revised upward to around 3.7% in the revised economic outlook scheduled for November.
Major overseas institutional investors are also raising their growth rate forecasts for the South Korean economy. According to the International Finance Center, as of the end of last month, the average forecast for this year’s growth rate from eight overseas investment banks (IBs) was 3.5%, up 0.2 percentage points from a month earlier. JPMorgan presented 4.0%, and Citi presented 3.8%. The OECD also raised its growth rate forecast to 3.7% last month.
Scenarios based on the fourth-quarter growth rate are also drawing attention. According to the Bank of Korea, the cumulative growth rate for the first three quarters of this year is 3.6% compared to the same period last year. Even if the fourth-quarter growth rate remains at 0% quarter-on-quarter, the annual growth rate will record 3.6%. If growth is around 0.5% in the fourth quarter, annual growth of 3.7% is also possible.
The possibility of 4% annual growth is also arithmetically open. Lee Dong-won, Director of the Economic Statistics Division 2 at the Bank of Korea, explained, “If growth exceeds 1.4% in the fourth quarter, 4% annual growth is also arithmetically possible.”
The growth trend appears likely to continue into the fourth quarter. The Bank of Korea expects semiconductor exports to maintain a favorable flow until next year and assessed that equipment investment is trending toward expansion to supply contracted volumes.
Government fiscal spending is also expected to boost fourth-quarter growth. This is because budgets whose execution was adjusted in the first half in preparation for a prolonged Middle East war are being executed in the second half. The Bank of Korea forecast that the execution of the annual planned budget will continue into the fourth quarter, acting positively on growth.
The growth outlook for next year is also bright. In August last month, the Bank of Korea forecast next year’s economic growth rate at 2.9%. Director Lee expected that the increase in semiconductor export volume growth would be higher than this year due to the effect of expanded production of HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) next year. However, he predicted that the rate of increase in semiconductor prices will slow compared to this year.
The variable going forward is private consumption. In the third quarter, consumption decreased due to temporary factors such as an automobile strike and stock market corrections, but it was assessed that passenger car consumption recovered significantly entering October. Cash dividends from semiconductor companies, performance bonuses paid in early next year, and expanded government transfer payments are also expected to support the recovery in consumption.
Director Lee said, “Exports and investment appear likely to maintain a favorable trend,” adding, “It will be important how much private consumption rebounds.”

articles.title: Power Equipment Stocks Rebound as AI Sentiment Revives - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Power Equipment Stocks Rebound as AI Sentiment Revives  Seoul Economic Daily

South Korean power equipment stocks rallied across the board on the 27th as investor sentiment toward the artificial intelligence industry recovered. Buying spread across AI-related shares on the local market after positive news from Anthropic triggered a rebound in U.S. technology stocks, while expectations of rising electricity demand from data center expansion and increased U.S. power grid investment supported gains in the power equipment sector.
According to the Korea Exchange, LS ELECTRIC (010120.KS) traded at 162,000 won during the session on the 27th, up 9,100 won, or 5.95%, from the previous session. Hyosung Heavy Industries (298040.KS) rose 4.37% to 1.934 million won, while HD Hyundai Electric (267260.KS) gained 4.36% to 466,500 won. LS (006260.KS) also traded up 5.25% at 220,500 won.
Buying extended to smaller power equipment names. Taihan Cable & Solution (001440.KS) climbed 7.33% to 21,950 won, and Iljin Electric (103590.KS) rose 6.75% to 58,500 won. Gaon Cable (000500.KS) advanced 6.39%, while Jeryong Electric (033100.KS) gained 5.53%, LS Eco Energy (229640.KQ) rose 4.80% and Daewon Cable (006340.KS) added 3.86%. Vinatech (126340.KQ) surged 13.95%.
The rally in power equipment shares is attributed to a recovery in sentiment toward AI-related investment. Overnight on U.S. markets, technology stocks rebounded as Anthropic's initial public offering filing and news of expanded graphics processing unit investment by SpaceX revived expectations for growth and capital spending at AI companies. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 2.82%. In South Korea, large-cap chipmakers including Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK hynix (000660.KS) jumped, with buying then spreading across the broader AI value chain, including materials, parts and equipment suppliers as well as power infrastructure.
Expectations that the expansion of AI data centers will ultimately translate into grid investment are also underpinning sentiment in the sector. KB Securities projected that about 55% of the increase in U.S. peak power demand through 2030 will come from data centers. With both power plants and large-scale electricity consumers growing at the same time, the physical bottleneck in the transmission networks linking them could persist until around 2030, according to the brokerage.
Korean companies are also expanding their North American businesses. Hyosung Heavy Industries holds a large share of the U.S. market for ultra-high-voltage transformers of 765 kilovolts and above and is increasing production capacity, while HD Hyundai Electric is winning more supply contracts for ultra-high-voltage and medium- to low-voltage transformers from big tech firms. Jung Hye-jung, an analyst at KB Securities, said that despite concerns about a slowdown in the pace of AI data center investment, there has been no change to the structural growth drivers of surging U.S. peak power demand and the replacement of aging grids.

articles.title: Korea's Per Capita Income Set to Top $40,000 for First Time in 12 Years - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Korea's Per Capita Income Set to Top $40,000 for First Time in 12 Years  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
South Korea's per capita gross national income is all but certain to cross the $40,000 threshold this year, the government said on the 27th, after the economy posted surprise growth of 1.0% in the third quarter.
In materials released after the Bank of Korea published its advance estimate of third-quarter real gross domestic product, the Ministry of Finance and Economy said per capita GNI would rise from the $30,000 range to the $40,000 range for the first time in 12 years. The ministry attributed the shift to two favorable factors since it unveiled its second-half economic growth strategy in July: a stronger won against the dollar (a lower won-dollar exchange rate) and an upgraded forecast for nominal growth.
"National income, which had remained in the $30,000 range, now appears set to move into the $40,000 range," Yoo Byung-hee, director general of the ministry's economic policy bureau, said at a briefing. "What is encouraging is that there is momentum for it to rise further."
Applying the International Monetary Fund's forecast of 21.7% nominal GDP growth this year and an average won-dollar rate of 1,463 won through September, the ministry estimated per capita GNI at about $43,500. If the exchange rate holds at the lower 1,300-won level for the rest of the year, the figure could reach $44,000, it said.
The ministry also noted that the IMF projects South Korea's per capita GDP at $44,000 this year, $49,000 next year and $52,000 in 2028.
Nominal GDP also expanded sharply in the third quarter, the ministry said. It projected annual nominal GDP growth of more than 20%, well above its initial forecast of 12.3%.
Real growth could reach the mid-3% range for the full year, the ministry said, as solid momentum has continued despite a high base in the first half.
Private consumption, which fell in the third quarter, should return to growth in the fourth quarter because the underlying recovery trend remains intact, the ministry said. Cash dividends from semiconductor companies in the fourth quarter and performance bonuses in the first quarter of next year will support the pickup in spending, it added.
Still, critics say the warmth of growth led by semiconductor exports has yet to spread sufficiently across domestic demand. The ministry acknowledged that structural problems such as polarization between sectors persist, along with continued pressure on household budgets from prices and other costs.
"We will step up efforts to stabilize livelihoods and ease polarization so that the warmth of growth reaches the lives of all citizens," the ministry said.

articles.title: Korea bill boosts megaprojects as SK eases equity load and GS expands PPAs - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Korea bill boosts megaprojects as SK eases equity load and GS expands PPAs  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
With the government and the ruling party pushing legislation to support large-scale regional investment, major groups' investments are expected to gain momentum. The special wide-area zone bill under discussion focuses on easing regulations that have hindered corporations' fundraising and power transaction to support the "three major megaprojects" in semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, and physical AI.
If the bill passes, SK is expected to be able to ease its investment burden by attracting outside capital. GS could broaden its options for procuring power if power purchase agreements (PPAs) for direct power transactions are expanded.
◇ SK's semiconductor investment burden would ease if equity rules are relaxed
According to the business community and political circles on the 27th, the leadership of the Democratic Party of Korea said at the supreme council meeting on the 22nd that it would push the "special wide-area zone bill" as the top legislative priority for the regular session. The ruling party's chief secretaries on the National Policy Committee, the Trade. Industry Energy. SMEs. and Startups Committee, and the Climate, Energy, Environment and Labor Committee will each sponsor the bill, and the policy committee chair and members of the relevant standing committees will join as co-sponsors.
The bill covers everything from easing investment regulations to support for power supply and rates, as well as labor exceptions. A Democratic Party policy committee official said it was "all-around legislative support."
The bill by National Policy Committee lawmaker Park Sang-hyuk lowers the mandatory equity holding in jointly invested semiconductor corporations from 100% to 50% and provides financial and tax support and regulatory exceptions for corporations in the special zones. It also includes labor exceptions, such as exempting high-income research and development personnel from the 52-hour workweek rule.
The bill by Climate, Energy and Environment Committee lawmaker Choi Ki-sang differs in that it excludes special provisions related to working hours and fixed-term employment from Park's bill, in consideration of labor opposition. The party leadership plans to review the two bills together to allow for social discussion.
If the bill passes, SK hynix is expected to reduce its investment burden by attracting outside investment or sharing investment costs.
Under the current Fair Trade Act, in a general holding company structure, a grandchild company must hold 100% of the total number of issued shares to own equity in a domestic great-grandchild company. If SK hynix, a grandchild of SK Co., Ltd., establishes a separate entity to build a semiconductor plant in Korea, SK hynix must own 100% of the equity in this entity, which would become a great-grandchild company of SK Co., Ltd.
In contrast, under the special law, SK hynix would need to hold only 50% equity in a jointly invested semiconductor corporation that meets certain requirements. In building a Honam semiconductor fab (plant), it would be able to tap funds from other corporations or financial institutions. That would also expand its capacity to invest funds in other production facilities or technology development.
◇ GS would benefit if coal-fired power is included in PPAs
Industry Committee lawmaker Jeong Jin-uk plans to introduce a bill this month to expand the scope of direct power transactions via power purchase agreements (PPAs), provide up to a 50% discount on electricity rates for corporations moving into the special zones, and exempt them from contributions to the Electric Power Industry Infrastructure Fund.
The business community is watching the scope of the PPA expansion. A power purchase agreement is a method in which a power generator and a power-using corporation directly set transaction terms such as supply volume and price.
Currently, direct PPAs are possible only for renewable energy such as solar and wind. The Democratic Party is considering expanding PPA eligibility to include nuclear and liquefied natural gas (LNG) power and is also reviewing whether to include coal-fired power. Including coal power could clash with the government's carbon neutrality policy, but given President Lee Jae-myung's repeated calls for a "speed race and leadership race," some within the party say there is a need to clearly widen the PPA scope.
GS Group's AI data center procurement strategy could change depending on whether direct transactions for coal-fired power are allowed. GS Donghae Power, an affiliate of GS, operates the Bukpyeong coal-fired power plant with a capacity of 1.19 gigawatts (GW) in Donghae, Gangwon. GS is also building an AI data center in the same area with a first-phase capacity of 1.2 GW and a long-term capacity of 2.4 GW.
For now, the project is premised on power supply through Korea Electric Power Corporation. If PPAs are allowed for coal-fired power, GS could also consider directly supplying electricity from its affiliated power plant to the data center. Power generators would secure long-term buyers, and data centers could diversify their power procurement sources.
Even if coal-fired power is excluded from PPAs, allowing direct transactions for LNG power would give corporations participating in the megaprojects new options. SK Group may leverage the LNG power generation business of its affiliate SK Innovation E&S, and GS Group may utilize GS EPS's LNG power business.
Other corporations could also expect benefits from support for power supply and infrastructure. Samsung Electronics is pushing investment in a Honam semiconductor production facility and a post-processing semiconductor facility in the Chungcheong region. For Samsung Electronics, building infrastructure within the special zone and streamlined licensing procedures could reduce investment expense burdens. Naver, which is pursuing the construction of a 1 GW AI data center, is also cited as a beneficiary of power supply and rate support.
A business community official said, "If the special wide-area zone bill under discussion passes, corporations will be able to drastically reduce their investment burden," adding, "The effect of expanding investment through deregulation appears likely to be greater than ever."
