[Lee Jae-yong: Four Years as Chairman] From Crisis to Semiconductor Superboom... Samsung Reclaims Its Strength Through Technology
Management Overhaul Amid Calls for Serious Self-Examination
Reclaiming the Global No. 1 Spot with Next-Generation Memory
Sustainable Competitiveness and Labor Relations Remain Challenges
Marking his fourth anniversary as chairman, Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong is reaping the rewards of restored technological competitiveness amid a semiconductor boom. Although the company faced delays in responding to high-bandwidth memory (HBM) demand and a semiconductor downturn, management overhauls and the adoption of advanced processes laid the groundwork for a turnaround. The supply of next-generation HBM, together with an AI-driven memory supercycle, has added momentum to its renewed growth.
On the 27th, his fourth anniversary as chairman, Lee is reportedly set to visit the RX Business Promotion Office at Samsung Electronics’ research and development (R&D) campus in Umyeon-dong, Seocho-gu, Seoul, without holding a separate commemorative event. He is expected to inspect precision-control technologies for robotic arms and hands.
Reforms After HBM Missteps... "We Must Invest for the Future"
Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jaeyong delivers welcoming remarks at the gala dinner for the KH Collection touring exhibition at the British Museum in London, England, on October 30 (local time). Samsung Electronics.
View original image
Samsung Electronics’ path to the current boom has not been smooth. Since Lee became chairman, the company has faced challenges as the AI semiconductor market was reshaped. It failed to respond to HBM demand in time and struggled to secure quality certification for HBM3E and expand supply while NVIDIA positioned SK hynix as a key supplier.
"Samsung Electronics was slow to invest in HBM and respond to market changes because it focused on the high profitability of its existing products," said Kim Yong-seok, a distinguished professor at Gachon University’s College of Semiconductor Engineering. Last year, SK hynix surpassed Samsung Electronics for the first time, posting KRW 47.2063 trillion in operating profit compared with Samsung Electronics’ KRW 43.6011 trillion.
Lee overhauled the company’s personnel and technology strategies. In May 2024, he appointed Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun as head of the Device Solutions (DS) Division, and at the end of the year, also put him in charge of the Memory Business. He appointed President Han Jin-man to head the Foundry Business and created the position of chief technology officer (CTO).
In March last year, Lee urged the company to "start with a thorough self-examination by the management" and said it "must invest for the future, even if that means sacrificing immediate profits." In December of the same year, he called on employees at the Giheung and Hwaseong campuses to "restore our fundamental technological competitiveness through bold innovation and investment."
Advanced Process Bets Pay Off... A Comeback Fueled by the Boom
HBM4 is at the center of the technological recovery. Samsung Electronics has improved speed and power efficiency by using sixth-generation (1c) DRAM in the 10-nanometer class (1 nm = one-billionth of a meter) and a 4-nanometer base die made by its own foundry, or contract semiconductor manufacturing, business. After beginning mass production and shipments in February this year, the company supplied customers with samples of 12-layer HBM4E in May.
Samsung Electronics also regained its position as the world’s leading company in DRAM revenue in the fourth quarter of last year, after ceding the top spot to SK hynix in the first quarter. A revamp of its technology, expanded AI investment and rising memory prices all contributed to the rebound.
Its integrated device manufacturer (IDM) model is also considered a strength. "Maintaining the foundry business despite pressure to sell or spin it off was an important management decision," said Kim Yang-paeng, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade. "Had the foundry business been spun off or sold, the company would have lost its next-generation advanced packaging technologies and foundational infrastructure as a whole."
Lee Jong-hwan, a professor in the Department of System Semiconductor Engineering at Sangmyung University, also said, "Samsung Electronics is the only company in the world capable of manufacturing both memory and non-memory semiconductors." He added, "If its foundry business can improve its results a little more, it could become a top-tier company."
Fifth Year as Chairman: Consolidate Its Technological Lead and Broaden Growth Foundations
The next challenge is to turn the current boom’s gains into sustainable competitiveness. In memory, the company must widen its technological lead to prepare for competition from China; in foundry, it must improve yields and expand its customer base. It also needs to strengthen its system semiconductor design capabilities, foster cooperation between its finished-products (DX) and semiconductor (DS) divisions, and build stable labor-management relations.
Another challenge is to extend its memory competitiveness in the AI market to finished products and services. Researcher Kim said the company needs to expand its business areas while leveraging its strengths as a memory supplier, adding, "It must drive innovation in finished products."

Why TSMC Is Seeking Rare-Earth-Free Equipment as China Tightens Its Grip
By CommonWealth Magazine
web only
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world's largest contract chipmaker, is exploring ways to reduce its reliance on rare-earth components in factory equipment as China's export controls raise concerns about potential disruptions to advanced semiconductor production.
According to an October 22 Reuters exclusive, three people familiar with the matter said TSMC had asked suppliers about using motors that do not require rare-earth magnets in its factory automation equipment.
The discussions remain preliminary, and no broad replacement program has been reported. TSMC did not comment on the Reuters report.
The development raises an important question: If rare earths account for only a small portion of the materials used in semiconductor manufacturing, why is the world's most advanced chipmaker looking for alternatives?
The answer lies in the distinction between the materials used to manufacture chips and the machinery needed to keep semiconductor factories operating.
China's rare-earth restrictions may have a limited direct impact on semiconductor production, but they can still create vulnerabilities in the equipment supply chain.
How does China's control of rare earths affect semiconductor equipment?
China's influence over the rare-earth supply chain extends well beyond mining.
In an earlier CommonWealth investigation into China's rare-earth leverage, industry experts explained that China's strongest position lies in refining and processing, where it controls much of the world's capacity.
Even rare-earth minerals extracted outside China may still pass through Chinese processing facilities before becoming usable industrial materials.
This creates dependencies across several stages of production.
A semiconductor equipment supplier may source motors from another country, while the magnets inside those motors rely on materials refined or manufactured in China.
Restrictions on rare-earth exports can therefore affect international manufacturers that do not purchase their raw materials directly from Chinese mining companies.
For chipmakers, the potential consequences extend beyond higher component prices.
A shortage of qualified replacement parts could complicate equipment maintenance, expansion, or procurement.
However, the scale of that risk depends on which components are affected, how much inventory suppliers maintain, and whether alternative products meet semiconductor manufacturing requirements.
Not every rare-earth restriction has the same impact on every piece of equipment.
Can TSMC replace rare-earth magnets with alternative motors?
Potentially, but replacing a component in a semiconductor manufacturing environment is not simply a matter of purchasing a different motor.
Rare-earth permanent magnets are widely used because they can provide strong magnetic performance in compact, efficient designs.
Alternative motor technologies may avoid certain rare-earth materials, but their suitability depends on the equipment's requirements.
Engineers must consider factors such as size, precision, energy efficiency, heat generation, reliability, and compatibility with existing machinery.
In semiconductor manufacturing, changes to equipment may also require extensive qualification before deployment.
Taiwan already has companies developing technologies that could help reduce reliance on rare-earth materials.
CommonWealth reported in May 2025 that Taiwanese manufacturer TECO Electric had developed motors that do not require rare earths.
Such technologies demonstrate that alternatives exist, although they do not establish that any particular motor is qualified for use in TSMC's semiconductor equipment.
Reuters did not identify which suppliers TSMC had approached or specify which alternative motor technologies were under consideration.
It remains unclear whether the company's discussions will lead to widespread equipment changes.
Taiwan wants to produce half its own rare-earth needs by 2030
Alongside the industry's search for substitutes, Taiwan is pursuing a separate strategy: developing domestic rare-earth processing and production capabilities.
On October 24, Taiwan's Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) disclosed plans to establish a demonstration facility capable of producing approximately 500 metric tons of rare-earth materials annually by the end of 2030.
According to Taiwan's Central News Agency, ITRI President Chang Pei-zen said the proposed output could meet about half of Taiwan's domestic demand.
The institute currently operates an experimental production line with an annual output of approximately five metric tons.
Reaching the proposed target would therefore require increasing output by roughly 100 times.
ITRI aims to complete construction of the demonstration facility by the end of 2028, then refine production processes and work toward the 2030 capacity target.
The project remains in the planning stage.
Funding arrangements, potential government support for private investors, and the commercial model have not been finalized.
The technical challenge is also substantial.
Rare-earth elements have similar chemical properties, making separation and purification complex. Producing high-quality materials at industrial scale requires specialized processes, equipment, and expertise.
The proposed facility represents an effort to build capabilities that Taiwan currently lacks at scale, rather than an immediate solution to the semiconductor industry's supply-chain concerns.
It is also important to distinguish the new production target from earlier, narrower estimates of rare-earth demand for specific industrial uses. The announced 500-ton capacity goal and the estimate that it could meet half of domestic demand refer to a broader planned production scope; they should not be directly compared with figures for semiconductor-specific consumption.
Can Taiwan reduce its dependence on China's rare earths?
Taiwan has several potential ways to reduce its exposure to Chinese rare-earth supply restrictions.
One is to diversify sources of raw materials and processed products.
Another is to develop local separation, refining, recycling, and magnet-production capabilities.
A third is technological substitution, including motors and equipment designed to operate without certain rare-earth materials.
Each approach addresses a different part of the supply chain.
Diversification can reduce dependence on a single supplier or country, but alternative suppliers may still rely on Chinese processing.
Domestic production could provide greater control over selected materials, but building industrial-scale capacity takes time and investment.
Substitution could eliminate the need for certain restricted materials altogether, although alternatives must meet the demanding technical standards of their intended applications.
Taiwan is also working with international partners to strengthen critical-mineral supply chains.
Reuters reported that the United States has expressed interest in ITRI's rare-earth development efforts as Washington and Taipei explore ways to diversify supply and processing capacity.
For Taiwan's semiconductor industry, the goal is not necessarily to replace every imported rare-earth component.
It is to ensure that a restriction affecting a relatively small but critical component does not become a bottleneck for an industry central to the global technology economy.
FAQs
Does TSMC use rare earths?
Rare-earth materials are used in certain industrial equipment components, including permanent magnets in motors. Reuters reported that TSMC is exploring motors that do not require rare-earth components for factory automation equipment.
Why is TSMC looking for rare-earth-free equipment?
According to Reuters, TSMC has consulted suppliers about alternatives as a precaution against potential disruptions caused by China's rare-earth export controls. The discussions are preliminary.
Could China stop Taiwan from making advanced chips by restricting rare earths?
China's controls could create equipment supply-chain risks, but there is no evidence that they have stopped TSMC's advanced chip production. The impact depends on affected components, inventories, alternative suppliers, and equipment qualification.
Can semiconductor factories operate without rare-earth magnets?
Some alternative motor technologies do not require rare-earth magnets. However, whether they can replace existing components depends on the equipment's technical and operational requirements.
Does Taiwan produce its own rare earths?
Taiwan has experimental rare-earth production and processing capabilities. ITRI is planning a demonstration facility targeting annual output of 500 metric tons by the end of 2030, but the project has not yet reached commercial scale.
Why does China dominate the rare-earth supply chain?
China has a particularly strong position in rare-earth processing and refining, not just mining. This makes international manufacturers dependent on Chinese supply-chain stages even when raw materials originate elsewhere.
The Bottom Line
TSMC's reported search for rare-earth-free equipment does not contradict earlier assessments that Taiwan's semiconductor industry has relatively limited direct demand for rare-earth materials.
Instead, it reveals another dimension of supply-chain risk.

articles.title: SK Hynix, Kioxia and the Geopolitics of Chipmaking - Technology Magazine
articles.summary: SK Hynix, Kioxia and the Geopolitics of Chipmaking  Technology Magazine
articles.full_text:
Six years after buying into its fiercest rival Kioxia’s backyard, SK Hynix is turning a historic cross-border alliance into hard cash.
This high-profile divestment spotlights the shifting financial and geopolitical dynamics across the global memory market.
In response to reports that it may distribute a special dividend of approximately ₩16tn (US$12bn), the South Korean chipmaker is preparing to detail its next wave of shareholder returns.
The prospective windfall stems directly from the company’s exit from the Japanese memory manufacturer. The sale marks the culmination of an improbable cross-border tie forged during a pivotal era for Asian semiconductor manufacturing.
SK Hynix originally entered into business with Kioxia in 2018. The company committed roughly ₩4tn (US$3.02bn) to join an international consortium led by private equity firm Bain Capital.
Bringing together investors from South Korea, Japan and the US, the consortium moved to back Japan’s premier flash memory asset after Kioxia separated from Toshiba to become an independent manufacturer.
- KRW16tn (US$12bn): Value of the potential special dividend SK Hynix is considering following the sale of its Kioxia stake
- KRW40tn (US$30.1bn): Value of own shares the company previously pledged to repurchase and cancel
- More than 50%: Proportion of free cash flow generated between 2025 and 2027 committed to boosting shareholder returns
An unlikely cross-border alliance
The partnership established a rare collaborative bridge across two competing semiconductor markets.
While South Korean chipmakers and Japanese technology firms have historically maintained an intense industrial rivalry, the consortium created a structure where regional players shared investment exposure.
This multi-nation arrangement allowed SK Hynix to secure a strategic stake in Japanese memory infrastructure. The consortium framework also enabled global partners to navigate complex trade relationships and regional market sensitivities.
The roots of the alliance trace directly to Toshiba, the pioneer of NAND flash memory that had long anchored Japan’s high-technology manufacturing pride.
Confronted with massive corporate restructuring, Toshiba spun off its prized memory chip unit into an independent business that eventually rebranded as Kioxia.
Guided by our mission to ‘uplift the world with ‘memory,’’ Kioxia aspires to transform the ‘memory’ created by people and society into new value that shapes the future. The name ‘Kioxia’ reflects this enduring commitment to harnessing the power of memory to enrich lives and contribute to the advancement of society
For SK Hynix, backing the carve-out provided an indirect foothold in a former Toshiba stronghold without triggering prohibitive antitrust backlash.
The deal transformed a legendary Japanese conglomerate asset into an internationally backed competitor, permanently reshaping Asian technology supply chains.
Although SK Hynix has kept specific financial figures private regarding the stake sale completed earlier this year, analysts calculate that the transaction delivered hefty cumulative gains.
The divestment untangles a long-standing cross-border tie and converts an illiquid equity position into deployable capital.
The transaction concludes a major chapter in regional memory alliances. South Korean newspaper Dong-A Ilbo reports that the exit now directly enables SK Hynix to consider a special dividend of about KRW16tn (US$12bn).
- KRW4tn: Initial capital committed by SK Hynix in 2018 to join the Bain Capital-led consortium backing Kioxia
- Six years: Span of the cross-border investment tie between SK Hynix and Kioxia, run from 2018 until the recent divestment
- Two decades: Time elapsed since the early-2000s debt crisis that pushed SK Hynix to the brink of bankruptcy
Balancing windfalls against market uncertainty
The potential special dividend arrives amid mounting pressure on advanced component manufacturers.
Alongside fellow supplier Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix generates record profits driven by surging AI memory demand.
Both Korean suppliers provide critical hardware to key platform customers such as NVIDIA. However, equity markets have grown increasingly cautious about long-term semiconductor capital expenditure.
Investor pressure also intensified after share prices plunged from record highs reached in June. The sharp decline stemmed partly from concerns over whether AI spending by US technology companies will remain durable.
To reinforce confidence amongst investors, SK Hynix had previously pledged to repurchase and cancel KRW40tn (US$30.1bn) of its own shares. The firm also plans to allocate more than 50% of free cash flow generated between 2025 and 2027 to boost returns.
Reshaping the industry
The potential cash return caps an extraordinary corporate turnaround for the South Korean chipmaker. Two decades ago, SK Hynix was reeling through a severe debt crisis that left the business nearly bankrupt.
Surging demand for high-bandwidth memory has since catapulted the business into the top tier of international tech valuations. The firm’s technological lead in AI hardware has dramatically altered competitive dynamics against long-standing industry peers.
That momentum culminated in SK Hynix overtaking arch-rival Samsung Electronics in market capitalisation to become South Korea’s most valuable listed chipmaker.
The milestone marked the first time the company claimed the premier spot on the national exchange.
The sudden shift in domestic leadership illustrates how specialised memory dominance has rewritten market fundamentals across East Asia. Monetising early strategic investments now provides the liquidity needed to defend that advantage.
Strategic pauses and capital allocation
Market volatility and regulatory oversight continue to reshape corporate roadmaps across the supply chain. SK Hynix states that it paused a planned US listing for its Solidigm storage unit due to ongoing market volatility.
The decision to pause the listing follows investor and regulatory concerns that had previously weighed on company shares. The pause allows the company to refocus its resources on core memory operations.
When asked about the special dividend report by the stock exchange operator, SK Hynix confirmed that it is “reviewing various shareholder return measures”. Reuters reported that the company plans to formally announce these initiatives alongside its third-quarter earnings.
While broader South Korean shares fell 1.3%, SK Hynix shares firmed up 0.5%. The performance reflects keen market focus on how balance-sheet distributions will influence wider memory strategies.
- Kioxia: This Japanese semiconductor manufacturer designs and produces advanced NAND flash memory chips and solid-state storage devices. Previously operating as the memory division of Toshiba, the company provides essential non-volatile data storage components to global hardware manufacturers, cloud data centres and consumer electronics brands operating across international computing and digital infrastructure markets.
- Samsung Electronics: This South Korean multinational technology business designs and produces advanced semiconductor memory solutions, mobile devices and consumer appliances. Operating as one of the largest chipmakers globally, the firm manufactures dynamic random-access memory and flash storage hardware, serving as a primary component supplier to hyperscale cloud providers and global computing device manufacturers.
- NVIDIA: This US technology corporation designs advanced graphics processing units, accelerated computing architectures and specialised software platforms. The company produces high-performance AI accelerator chips used to train and run complex machine learning models across global data centres, relying on ultra-fast, high-bandwidth memory products supplied by international semiconductor manufacturing partners to power operations.
- Bain Capital: This US private equity and alternative asset management firm manages multi-asset investments across private equity, venture capital and credit markets globally. The firm structures strategic corporate transactions and buyouts across multiple industries, having orchestrated the multi-billion-dollar international investor consortium that acquired and established Kioxia as an independent Japanese memory company.
- SK Hynix: This South Korean semiconductor manufacturer produces dynamic random-access memory and flash storage chips for global hardware markets. Operating as a major component supplier to international cloud and computing giants, the company delivers high-bandwidth memory hardware that powers advanced AI accelerators, data centres and consumer electronics devices worldwide.

Goldman Sachs has identified betting against the U.S. dollar in favor of the Japanese yen as a potential hedge against an artificial intelligence-driven stock market selloff.
Bloomberg reported that strategists, including Kamakshya Trivedi, outlined the strategy in an October 23 note. The recommendation followed renewed selling across global technology stocks, which pushed investors toward assets traditionally favored during market uncertainty.
Goldman Sachs expects the yen to offer stronger protection when concerns about economic growth trigger simultaneous declines in stocks and government bond yields.
The strategists wrote that 'the yen now looks like a more attractive hedge' for portfolios exposed to economic cycles. However, they cautioned that broader global conditions could still put downward pressure on the Japanese currency.
Their preferred longer-term strategy involves selling the U.S. dollar against the yen, commonly known as shorting USD/JPY. Such a position gains value when the yen strengthens relative to the dollar.
'Short USD/JPY should be the most effective hedge,' the strategists wrote, referring to broader economic weakness or a potential AI-related market shock.
For now, Goldman Sachs favors selling the euro against the yen. The bank expects limited near-term support for a sustained yen rally and sees little chance of an unexpectedly aggressive message from the Bank of Japan at its October meeting.
The recommendation follows a retreat in Japanese equities as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending.
Japan's Nikkei 225 closed at 62,693.16 on October 23, approximately 14% below its reported record level. Semiconductor and other technology-related companies contributed to the decline.
Selling continued on October 26, when the Nikkei dropped another 0.80% to 62,189.65, its lowest closing level since July 30.
Meanwhile, the yen gained 0.9% against the U.S. dollar on October 22 as Treasury yields declined. It reached its strongest level in more than a month the following day before surrendering some gains.
Goldman's assessment comes as concerns over AI investment spread across financial markets. A recent Bank of Korea warning addressed risks associated with borrowing and leveraged investments linked to semiconductor and AI stocks.
The bank believes falling U.S. stock prices and bond yields could favor the yen, based on its historical performance during periods of weaker economic expectations.
Goldman Sachs linked its changing assessment to Japan's monetary policy. The Bank of Japan has moved away from the policies that previously kept domestic borrowing costs unusually low.
The BOJ currently maintains its policy rate near 1.25%. Goldman said the yen has become less sensitive to rising global yields than it was during the previous six to seven years.
However, borrowing in yen to fund investments in higher-yielding assets remains an important market consideration. Previous episodes of yen strength have raised concerns about the unwinding of yen carry trades.
Attention now turns to the Federal Reserve's October 27–28 meeting and the Bank of Japan's October 29–30 policy meeting.
The Fed is widely expected to leave rates unchanged in October, while markets anticipate possible increases by both central banks in December.
According to the BOJ's official schedule, its next policy announcement will come on October 30. The Federal Reserve will announce its decision on October 28, alongside a press conference.
The banks will then meet again in December, with the Federal Reserve's final 2026 meeting scheduled for December 8–9 and the BOJ's for December 17–18.

This investment is significant in that global semiconductor equipment companies highly appreciated the industrial competitiveness of southern Gyeonggi Province. Excelis finally chose Gyeonggi Province after reviewing its investment location in Korea, Singapore and Malaysia.
In order to attract investment, Gyeonggi Province has supported meeting with executives at its U.S. headquarters, finding suitable sites, and consulting on licensing. After signing a contract to move into the Oseong foreign investment area in Pyeongtaek in September, Excelis began to create facilities in earnest with the start of the construction.
Xcelis is a global semiconductor equipment company based in Massachusetts, United States. The representative product, 'Purion' series, is used in ion implantation processes that precisely control the electrical characteristics of semiconductors. It also has high technology in the field of silicon carbide (SiC) power semiconductors used in electric vehicles and industrial power devices.
"As much as you trusted and invested in Gyeonggi-do, we will repay that belief with solid results," Gyeonggi-do Province Governor Choo Mi-ae said. "We will work closely with the central government and related agencies to secure stable power and water, and prove it with results so that global companies can choose Gyeonggi-do without hesitation."
On the other hand, about 50 officials from major customer companies including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix attended the groundbreaking ceremony, including Governor Choo, Pyeongtaek Mayor Choi Won-yong, CEO of Excelis Russell Lo, and Excelis Korea CEO Park Young-geun.
